**Direct answer:** No. Idempotency keys make retries safe only within a limited window and only if the retry is the same request. Stripe documents a window explicitly. For AWS I confirmed the same-parameters rule, but I did not confirm a retention period. This is a partial answer, since I stopped after five source retrievals and some claims rest on a single source.

**Stripe (API v1)**
- Stripe may delete v1 keys automatically once they are at least 24 hours old. If you reuse a key after it has been deleted, Stripe treats it as a new request, so a late retry can repeat the operation. The 24 hours is a minimum age, not a guaranteed retention period. https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests
- Stripe saves the status code and body of the first request made with a key, once endpoint execution begins. Retries return the saved response, including 500 errors. https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests
- Stripe does not save a result when the parameters fail validation or the request conflicts with one already running. Those requests can be retried. https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests
- Keys can be up to 255 characters, and Stripe suggests V4 UUIDs or another high-entropy random string. https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests
- API v2 behaves differently: retries don't repeat successful operations, and Stripe completes failed or partly failed work when it can. I did not find a v2 key-expiry figure. https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests

**AWS**
- AWS says that if a request arrives with a client request token it has already seen but with different parameters, it returns a validation error for a parameter mismatch. To support this, AWS stores the original request's parameters with the token. https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/
- The same article has a section titled "Late arriving requests and the life span of unique client request identifiers." So AWS treats token lifetime as a real design limit. The excerpt I retrieved was cut off before any figure. https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/
- The AWS SDK and CLI generate a client token and reuse it across retries for operations that support idempotency. https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/
- EC2 and ECS docs say not to retry a 200 or a 400-series error, and to retry 500-series errors with backoff. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ec2/latest/devguide/ec2-api-idempotency.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/ECS_Idempotency.html

**Not established**
- I did not confirm an AWS retention period for tokens. A search summary said the ECS RunTask token TTL is 24 hours and that EC2 tokens are limited to 64 ASCII characters. The pages I fetched showed only the retry table, so I'm not relying on those figures. Check them on the ECS and EC2 API reference pages before using them.
- I did not read any source that argues against these points, and no claim here has a second independent source.

**Comparison:** Both vendors tie idempotency to the same request, since changed parameters are rejected or treated as a different intent. Both also make the guarantee time-limited. Stripe states a specific 24-hour minimum for v1, and AWS flags token lifetime as a design concern. Neither source supports retrying forever. After the window, check what actually happened (for example, look up the resource) before sending the request again.

Sources:
- https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests
- https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/
- https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ec2/latest/devguide/ec2-api-idempotency.html
- https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/ECS_Idempotency.html
